```{r setup}
#| include: false

# ── Packages used in this chapter ──────────────────────────────────
#   Rendered (knitr / build-time):  dplyr, plotly
#   WebR (in-browser cells):         dplyr, plotly, BSDA, infer
#     WebR packages must also be declared in the YAML `webr: packages`
#     block above so they load when the deck opens (see help.html).
# ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

library(dplyr)
library(plotly)
set.seed(258)

normal_pdf <- function(x) dnorm(x)
t_pdf <- function(x, df) dt(x, df)

tail_plot <- function(stat = 1.8, dist = "z", df = 12, alternative = "greater",
                      title = "Reference distribution") {
  x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)
  y <- if (dist == "z") normal_pdf(x) else t_pdf(x, df)
  stat_abs <- abs(stat)
  shade <- switch(
    alternative,
    greater = x >= stat,
    less = x <= stat,
    two = abs(x) >= stat_abs
  )
  p <- plot_ly(width = 520, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4),
              name = if (dist == "z") "N(0,1)" else paste0("t(", df, ")")) |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade], y = y[shade], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.32)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.9)", width = 1),
              name = "p-value area") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = FALSE,
                   range = c(-4, 4), fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 28),
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
  p
}

# Chi-square reference distribution with a shaded tail (for variance tests)
chisq_tail_plot <- function(stat, df, alternative = "greater",
                            title = "Chi-square reference") {
  x <- seq(0, qchisq(0.999, df), length.out = 500)
  y <- dchisq(x, df)
  shade <- if (alternative == "less") x <= stat else x >= stat
  plot_ly(width = 520, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4),
              name = paste0("chi^2(", df, ")")) |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade], y = y[shade], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.32)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.9)", width = 1),
              name = "p-value area") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#222",
                   rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 28),
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# Meaningful chi-square plot: draws the observed statistic, the critical value, and the
# rejection region -- the chi-square analog of ztest_plot / ttest_plot.
chisq_test_plot <- function(chistar, chicrit = NULL, df = 27, alternative = "greater",
                            title = "", shade = "pvalue") {
  xmax <- max(qchisq(0.999, df), chistar, chicrit) * 1.08  # room on the right tail
  x <- seq(0, xmax, length.out = 500)
  y <- dchisq(x, df)
  shade_at <- if (shade == "reject" && !is.null(chicrit)) chicrit else chistar
  shade_keep <- if (alternative == "less") x <= shade_at else x >= shade_at
  ymax <- max(y)
  # Draw the statistic line with a deliberate visual gap from the critical value so the two
  # markers are clearly distinguishable. This is schematic: the exact numbers live in the
  # labels and the calculation box, but the picture keeps the lines from piling up.
  gap <- 0.025 * xmax                         # small visual gap: close to crit, but distinct
  stat_x <- if (!is.null(chicrit)) {
    if (alternative == "less") max(chistar, chicrit + gap) else min(chistar, chicrit - gap)
  } else chistar
  cmark <- ymax * 0.80                        # tall line, clearly poking above the curve
  shapes <- list(
    list(type = "line", x0 = stat_x, x1 = stat_x, y0 = 0, y1 = cmark,
         line = list(color = "#333", width = 3))
  )
  # statistic label sits in the white space up-and-left of its line (right edge stops short
  # of the crit line), below the crit label, so it never lands on the curve or a marker
  anns <- list(
    list(x = stat_x, y = cmark + ymax * 0.22, xshift = -5,
         text = paste0("&#967;&#178;* = ", formatC(chistar, format = "f", digits = 2)),
         showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "right",
         font = list(color = "#333", size = 13))
  )
  if (!is.null(chicrit)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(
      list(type = "line", x0 = chicrit, x1 = chicrit, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.05,
           line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 2.5, dash = "dash"))))
    anns <- c(anns, list(
      list(x = chicrit, y = ymax * 1.27,
           text = paste0("crit. value = ", formatC(chicrit, format = "f", digits = 2)),
           showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center",
           font = list(color = "#00695c", size = 12))))
  }
  plot_ly(width = 520, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 3.5),
              name = paste0("chi^2(", df, ")"), hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade_keep], y = y[shade_keep], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.6)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)", width = 1),
              name = "shaded region", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = "test statistic", range = c(0, xmax),
                   zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#222", fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.3), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 42),
      showlegend = FALSE, shapes = shapes, annotations = anns
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# Meaningful F plot: draws the observed statistic, the critical value, and the rejection
# region -- the F analog of ztest_plot / ttest_plot / chisq_test_plot.
ftest_plot <- function(fstar, fcrit = NULL, df1 = 11, df2 = 9, alternative = "greater",
                       title = "", shade = "reject") {
  # Extend the axis so the statistic is drawn at its TRUE position (accurate), with a bit
  # of headroom so the statistic line and its label are not clipped at the right edge.
  xmax <- max(qf(0.99, df1, df2), fstar, fcrit) * 1.2
  x <- seq(0, xmax, length.out = 600)
  y <- df(x, df1, df2)
  ymax <- max(y)
  shade_at <- if (shade == "reject" && !is.null(fcrit)) fcrit else fstar
  shade_keep <- if (alternative == "less") x <= shade_at else x >= shade_at
  fmark <- max(df(fstar, df1, df2), ymax * 0.42)   # floor keeps the far-tail line visible
  shapes <- list(
    list(type = "line", x0 = fstar, x1 = fstar, y0 = 0, y1 = fmark,
         line = list(color = "#333", width = 3))
  )
  # statistic sits far out in the tail: label anchored left of its line, in the open tail
  anns <- list(
    list(x = fstar, y = fmark + ymax * 0.13, xshift = -8,
         text = paste0("F* = ", formatC(fstar, format = "f", digits = 2)),
         showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "right",
         font = list(color = "#333", size = 13))
  )
  if (!is.null(fcrit)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(
      list(type = "line", x0 = fcrit, x1 = fcrit, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 0.62,
           line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 2.5, dash = "dash"))))
    anns <- c(anns, list(
      list(x = fcrit, y = ymax * 0.70, xshift = 4,
           text = paste0("crit. value = ", formatC(fcrit, format = "f", digits = 2)),
           showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "left",
           font = list(color = "#00695c", size = 11))))
  }
  plot_ly(width = 520, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 3.5),
              name = paste0("F(", df1, ", ", df2, ")"), hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade_keep], y = y[shade_keep], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.6)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)", width = 1),
              name = "shaded region", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = "test statistic", range = c(0, xmax),
                   zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#222", fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.3), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 42),
      showlegend = FALSE, shapes = shapes, annotations = anns
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# Two cascading dropdowns: pick the type of test (Z / t / chi-square / F), then the
# alternative (left / right / both tails). The shaded p-value area updates for the
# selected (distribution, tail) combination. Cascade logic runs in JS via onRender,
# since plotly's own dropdowns cannot AND two independent menus together.
test_dropdown <- function() {
  np <- 400
  df_t <- 11; df_c <- 12; f1 <- 11; f2 <- 9

  z_x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = np); z_y <- dnorm(z_x)
  t_x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = np); t_y <- dt(t_x, df_t)
  c_max <- qchisq(0.999, df_c)
  c_x <- seq(0, c_max, length.out = np); c_y <- dchisq(c_x, df_c)
  f_max <- qf(0.995, f1, f2)
  f_x <- seq(0, f_max, length.out = np); f_y <- df(f_x, f1, f2)

  # cdf grids let the JS side compute p-values by interpolation while dragging
  dists <- list(
    z     = list(x = z_x, y = z_y, cdf = pnorm(z_x),        symmetric = TRUE,  wname = "Z"),
    t     = list(x = t_x, y = t_y, cdf = pt(t_x, df_t),     symmetric = TRUE,  wname = "t"),
    chisq = list(x = c_x, y = c_y, cdf = pchisq(c_x, df_c), symmetric = FALSE, wname = "χ²"),
    F     = list(x = f_x, y = f_y, cdf = pf(f_x, f1, f2),   symmetric = FALSE, wname = "F")
  )

  # starting boundary position(s) for each (distribution, tail) combination
  s_sym <- 1.3
  inits <- list(
    z     = list(left = -s_sym, right = s_sym, both = c(-s_sym, s_sym)),
    t     = list(left = -s_sym, right = s_sym, both = c(-s_sym, s_sym)),
    chisq = list(left = qchisq(0.12, df_c), right = qchisq(0.88, df_c),
                 both = c(qchisq(0.05, df_c), qchisq(0.95, df_c))),
    F     = list(left = qf(0.12, f1, f2), right = qf(0.88, f1, f2),
                 both = c(qf(0.05, f1, f2), qf(0.95, f1, f2)))
  )

  tl <- function(dist, tail) {
    nm   <- switch(dist, z = "Z", t = "t", chisq = "Chi-square", F = "F")
    side <- switch(tail, left = "Left-tailed", right = "Right-tailed", both = "Two-tailed")
    paste0(side, " ", nm, " test — drag the dotted line")
  }
  titles <- list()
  for (d in names(dists))
    titles[[d]] <- list(left = tl(d, "left"), right = tl(d, "right"), both = tl(d, "both"))
  ranges <- list(z = c(-4, 4), t = c(-4, 4), chisq = c(0, c_max), F = c(0, f_max))

  pdata <- list(dists = dists, inits = inits, titles = titles, ranges = ranges)

  init_d <- dists$t
  fill_col <- "rgba(249,168,37,0.55)"; line_col <- "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)"

  p <- plot_ly(width = 1040, height = 310) |>
    add_lines(x = init_d$x, y = init_d$y,
              line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4),
              name = "reference", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = init_d$x, y = ifelse(init_d$x >= s_sym, init_d$y, 0),
              type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_col,
              line = list(color = line_col, width = 0),
              name = "p-value area", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = titles$t$right, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", range = c(-4, 4), zeroline = TRUE,
                   zerolinecolor = "#222", fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 30, b = 104),
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE,
           edits = list(shapePosition = TRUE))

  js <- "
  function(el, x, data) {
    var mk = function(label, opts, selv){
      var lab = document.createElement('label');
      lab.style.cssText='display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;color:#004d40;font-weight:700;font-family:Arial,sans-serif;font-size:15px;';
      var s = document.createElement('select');
      s.style.cssText='font-size:15px;padding:3px 8px;border:1px solid #00695c;border-radius:6px;background:#fff;color:#2f3437;font-family:Arial,sans-serif;';
      opts.forEach(function(o){var op=document.createElement('option');op.value=o.v;op.text=o.t;if(o.v===selv)op.selected=true;s.appendChild(op);});
      lab.appendChild(document.createTextNode(label)); lab.appendChild(s);
      return {lab:lab, sel:s};
    };
    var wrap = document.createElement('div');
    wrap.style.cssText='display:flex;gap:18px;justify-content:flex-end;align-items:center;margin:0 0 4px 0;';
    var dsel = mk('Type of test:', [{v:'z',t:'Z test'},{v:'t',t:'t test'},{v:'chisq',t:'Chi-square test'},{v:'F',t:'F test'}], 't');
    var tsel = mk('Alternative:', [{v:'left',t:'Left-tailed'},{v:'right',t:'Right-tailed'},{v:'both',t:'Two-tailed'}], 'right');
    wrap.appendChild(dsel.lab); wrap.appendChild(tsel.lab);
    el.parentNode.insertBefore(wrap, el);

    var interp = function(xs, ys, v){
      if (v <= xs[0]) return ys[0];
      if (v >= xs[xs.length-1]) return ys[ys.length-1];
      var lo = 0, hi = xs.length - 1;
      while (hi - lo > 1){ var m = (hi + lo) >> 1; if (xs[m] <= v) lo = m; else hi = m; }
      var f = (v - xs[lo]) / (xs[hi] - xs[lo]);
      return ys[lo] + f * (ys[hi] - ys[lo]);
    };
    var fmt  = function(v){ return (v < 0 ? '−' : '') + Math.abs(v).toFixed(2); };
    var fmtp = function(v){ return Math.max(0, Math.min(1, v)).toFixed(4); };

    var state = {d:'t', t:'right', b:[1.3]};
    var setDefaults = function(){
      var i = data.inits[state.d][state.t];
      state.b = Array.isArray(i) ? i.slice() : [i];
    };

    var redraw = function(live, moved){
      var dd = data.dists[state.d], xs = dd.x, ys = dd.y, cdf = dd.cdf;
      var keep;
      if (state.t === 'left'){ var vl = state.b[0]; keep = function(q){ return q <= vl; }; }
      else if (state.t === 'right'){ var vr = state.b[0]; keep = function(q){ return q >= vr; }; }
      else { var lo2 = state.b[0], hi2 = state.b[1]; keep = function(q){ return q <= lo2 || q >= hi2; }; }
      var sy = xs.map(function(q, i){ return keep(q) ? ys[i] : 0; });

      var shps = state.b.map(function(v){
        return {type:'line', x0:v, x1:v, y0:0, y1:interp(xs, ys, v),
                line:{color:'#b26a00', width:2.5, dash:'dot'}};
      });
      var anns = state.b.map(function(v, i){
        var lab = 'test statistic';
        if (dd.symmetric){
          if (state.t === 'both') lab = (i === 0 ? '−|test statistic|' : '|test statistic|');
          else if (state.t === 'left') lab = '−|test statistic|';
        }
        return {x:v, y:0, xref:'x', yref:'y', text:lab, showarrow:false,
                yanchor:'top', yshift:-20, font:{size:12, color:'#b26a00'},
                bgcolor:'rgba(255,255,255,0.75)'};
      });

      var w = dd.wname, txt;
      if (state.t === 'left'){
        var v1 = state.b[0], p1l = interp(xs, cdf, v1);
        txt = 'w* = ' + fmt(v1) + '    p-value = P(' + w + ' ≤ ' + fmt(v1) + ') = ' + fmtp(p1l);
      } else if (state.t === 'right'){
        var v2 = state.b[0], p1r = 1 - interp(xs, cdf, v2);
        txt = 'w* = ' + fmt(v2) + '    p-value = P(' + w + ' ≥ ' + fmt(v2) + ') = ' + fmtp(p1r);
      } else if (dd.symmetric){
        var sB = Math.abs(state.b[1]), pB = 2 * (1 - interp(xs, cdf, sB));
        txt = '|w*| = ' + fmt(sB) + '    p-value = 2·P(' + w + ' ≥ ' + fmt(sB) + ') = ' + fmtp(pB);
      } else {
        var loB = state.b[0], hiB = state.b[1];
        var pl = interp(xs, cdf, loB), pu = 1 - interp(xs, cdf, hiB);
        txt = 'p-value = P(' + w + ' ≤ ' + fmt(loB) + ') + P(' + w + ' ≥ ' + fmt(hiB) + ') = ' +
              fmtp(pl) + ' + ' + fmtp(pu) + ' = ' + fmtp(pl + pu);
      }
      anns.push({x:0.5, y:-0.5, xref:'paper', yref:'paper', text:txt, showarrow:false,
                 font:{size:14, color:'#2f3437'}, bgcolor:'rgba(245,246,247,0.95)',
                 bordercolor:'#d8dee2', borderwidth:1, borderpad:5});

      Plotly.restyle(el, {x:[xs], y:[sy]}, [1]);
      if (live){
        // During an active drag, only touch things that will not fight
        // Plotly's own drag of the grabbed line: the shaded fill (restyled
        // above), the p-value/labels, and — for symmetric two-tailed — the
        // mirrored boundary (the line the user is NOT holding).
        var upd = {annotations: anns};
        if (state.t === 'both' && moved != null){
          var other = 1 - moved;
          upd['shapes[' + other + '].x0'] = state.b[other];
          upd['shapes[' + other + '].x1'] = state.b[other];
          upd['shapes[' + other + '].y1'] = interp(xs, ys, state.b[other]);
        }
        Plotly.relayout(el, upd);
      } else {
        Plotly.restyle(el, {x:[xs], y:[ys]}, [0]);
        Plotly.relayout(el, {'title.text': data.titles[state.d][state.t],
                             'xaxis.range': data.ranges[state.d],
                             shapes: shps, annotations: anns});
      }
    };

    // inverse CDF: smallest x with cdf(x) >= p (cdf is increasing)
    var invinterp = function(cdf, xs, p){
      if (p <= cdf[0]) return xs[0];
      if (p >= cdf[cdf.length-1]) return xs[xs.length-1];
      var lo = 0, hi = cdf.length - 1;
      while (hi - lo > 1){ var m = (hi + lo) >> 1; if (cdf[m] <= p) lo = m; else hi = m; }
      var f = (p - cdf[lo]) / (cdf[hi] - cdf[lo]);
      return xs[lo] + f * (xs[hi] - xs[lo]);
    };

    var applyMove = function(moved, nx){
      var r = data.ranges[state.d];
      var dd = data.dists[state.d], xs = dd.x, cdf = dd.cdf;
      nx = Math.max(r[0] + 0.02, Math.min(r[1] - 0.02, nx));
      if (state.t === 'right'){
        // Z/t: the dotted line may not cross the centre (x = 0, the black line)
        if (dd.symmetric) nx = Math.max(0, nx);
        state.b = [nx];
      } else if (state.t === 'left'){
        if (dd.symmetric) nx = Math.min(0, nx);
        state.b = [nx];
      } else {
        if (dd.symmetric){
          // two boundaries are mirror images about 0, so 0 is never crossed
          var s = Math.max(0.02, Math.abs(nx));
          state.b = [-s, s];
        } else {
          // Equal-tail two-sided test for chi-square / F: each tail keeps the
          // same area, so dragging one boundary moves the other to the matching
          // quantile. The lower stays below the median, the upper above it.
          var med = invinterp(cdf, xs, 0.5);
          if (moved === 0){
            var xlo = Math.max(r[0] + 0.02, Math.min(nx, med - 0.02));
            var plo = interp(xs, cdf, xlo);
            state.b = [xlo, invinterp(cdf, xs, 1 - plo)];
          } else {
            var xhi = Math.min(r[1] - 0.02, Math.max(nx, med + 0.02));
            var pup = 1 - interp(xs, cdf, xhi);
            state.b = [invinterp(cdf, xs, pup), xhi];
          }
        }
      }
    };

    // Coalesce the rapid drag events into a single redraw per animation frame
    // so the line tracks the cursor smoothly instead of stuttering.
    var pending = null, rafId = null;
    var flush = function(){
      rafId = null;
      if (!pending) return;
      applyMove(pending.moved, pending.nx);
      redraw(true, pending.moved);
      pending = null;
    };

    var handleMove = function(ev, live){
      var moved = null, nx = null;
      Object.keys(ev || {}).forEach(function(k){
        var m = k.match(/^shapes\\[(\\d+)\\]\\.x0$/);
        if (m){ moved = +m[1]; nx = +ev[k]; }
      });
      if (moved === null || isNaN(nx)) return;
      if (live){
        pending = {moved: moved, nx: nx};
        if (rafId === null) rafId = window.requestAnimationFrame(flush);
      } else {
        pending = null;
        if (rafId !== null){ window.cancelAnimationFrame(rafId); rafId = null; }
        applyMove(moved, nx);
        redraw(false, moved);
      }
    };
    // plotly_relayouting fires continuously during the drag (smooth live
    // updates); plotly_relayout fires once on release (final full redraw).
    el.on('plotly_relayouting', function(ev){ handleMove(ev, true); });
    el.on('plotly_relayout',    function(ev){ handleMove(ev, false); });

    var onpick = function(){ state.d = dsel.sel.value; state.t = tsel.sel.value; setDefaults(); redraw(); };
    dsel.sel.addEventListener('change', onpick);
    tsel.sel.addEventListener('change', onpick);
    setDefaults(); redraw();
  }
  "
  htmlwidgets::onRender(p, js, data = pdata)
}

# Complete decision diagram: p-value area + critical value (alpha cutoff) + z*
decision_plot <- function(zstar, zalpha = 1.645, title = "") {
  x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)
  y <- dnorm(x)
  pval_idx <- x >= zstar
  ymax <- max(y)
  plot_ly(width = 560, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 3.5),
              name = "N(0,1)", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[pval_idx], y = y[pval_idx], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.55)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)", width = 1),
              name = "p-value", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = "test statistic", range = c(-4, 4),
                   zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.3), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 30, r = 10, t = 38, b = 30),
      showlegend = FALSE,
      shapes = list(
        list(type = "line", x0 = zalpha, x1 = zalpha, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.06,
             line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 2, dash = "dash")),
        list(type = "line", x0 = zstar, x1 = zstar, y0 = 0, y1 = dnorm(zstar),
             line = list(color = "#333", width = 2))
      ),
      annotations = list(
        list(x = zalpha, y = ymax * 1.17, text = "crit. value (α = 0.05)",
             showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center",
             font = list(color = "#00695c", size = 11)),
        list(x = zstar, y = dnorm(zstar) + 0.04, text = "z*", showarrow = FALSE,
             xanchor = "center", font = list(color = "#333", size = 13))
      )
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# Worked one-sided z-test diagram: marks z* (visible even far in the tail),
# shades the p-value, and draws the alpha critical value.
ztest_plot <- function(zstar, zcrit = NULL, alternative = "greater",
                       title = "", pval = NULL, shade = "pvalue") {
  # extra room on the tail side so z* and its centered label sit in open space (not clipped)
  xr <- if (alternative == "less") c(-5.5, 4) else c(-4, 5.5)
  x <- seq(xr[1], xr[2], length.out = 500)
  y <- dnorm(x)
  shade_at <- if (shade == "reject" && !is.null(zcrit)) zcrit else zstar
  shade_keep <- if (alternative == "less") x <= shade_at else x >= shade_at
  ymax <- max(y)
  zmark <- max(dnorm(zstar), 0.14)   # floor keeps z* visible out in the tail
  shapes <- list(
    list(type = "line", x0 = zstar, x1 = zstar, y0 = 0, y1 = zmark,
         line = list(color = "#333", width = 2.5))
  )
  # place the z* label on the tail side of its line so it clears the crit-value marker
  lab_anchor <- if (alternative == "less") "right" else "left"
  lab_shift  <- if (alternative == "less") -6 else 6
  anns <- list(
    list(x = zstar, y = zmark + 0.07,
         text = paste0("z* = ", formatC(zstar, format = "f", digits = 2)),
         showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = lab_anchor, xshift = lab_shift,
         font = list(color = "#333", size = 13))
  )
  if (!is.null(zcrit)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(
      list(type = "line", x0 = zcrit, x1 = zcrit, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.05,
           line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 2, dash = "dash"))))
    anns <- c(anns, list(
      list(x = zcrit, y = ymax * 1.17, text = "crit. value (α = 0.05)",
           showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center",
           font = list(color = "#00695c", size = 11))))
  }
  if (!is.null(pval)) {
    side <- if (alternative == "less") -3.05 else 3.05
    anns <- c(anns, list(
      list(x = side, y = 0.085, text = paste0("p-value ≈ ", pval),
           showarrow = TRUE, ax = if (alternative == "less") -10 else 10, ay = -28,
           arrowcolor = "#b26a00", font = list(color = "#b26a00", size = 12))))
  }
  plot_ly(width = 520, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 3.5),
              name = "N(0,1)", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade_keep], y = y[shade_keep], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.6)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)", width = 1),
              name = "shaded region", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = "test statistic", range = xr,
                   zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.3), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 34, r = 12, t = 36, b = 42),
      showlegend = FALSE, shapes = shapes, annotations = anns
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

ttest_plot <- function(tstar, tcrit = NULL, df = 11, alternative = "greater",
                       title = "", pval = NULL, shade = "pvalue") {
  # adaptive range: always leaves room for t* and its label so it is not clipped, even far out
  if (alternative == "less") {
    xr <- c(min(-5.5, tstar - 1.6), 4)
  } else if (alternative == "two.sided") {
    m <- max(5.5, abs(tstar) + 1.6); xr <- c(-m, m)
  } else {
    xr <- c(-4, max(5.5, tstar + 1.6))
  }
  x <- seq(xr[1], xr[2], length.out = 500)
  y <- dt(x, df)
  cut <- if (shade == "reject" && !is.null(tcrit)) abs(tcrit) else abs(tstar)
  shade_keep <- if (alternative == "less") x <= -cut else if (alternative == "two.sided") abs(x) >= cut else x >= cut
  ymax <- max(y)
  tmark <- max(dt(tstar, df), 0.14)   # floor keeps t* visible out in the tail
  shapes <- list(
    list(type = "line", x0 = tstar, x1 = tstar, y0 = 0, y1 = tmark,
         line = list(color = "#333", width = 2.5))
  )
  # label sits centered directly above the t* line; extended x-range keeps it inside the view
  anns <- list(
    list(x = tstar, y = tmark + 0.07,
         text = paste0("t* = ", formatC(tstar, format = "f", digits = 2)),
         showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center",
         font = list(color = "#333", size = 13))
  )
  if (!is.null(tcrit)) {
    tc <- abs(tcrit)
    crit_x <- if (alternative == "two.sided") c(-tc, tc) else if (alternative == "less") -tc else tc
    for (cx in crit_x) {
      shapes <- c(shapes, list(
        list(type = "line", x0 = cx, x1 = cx, y0 = 0, y1 = ymax * 1.05,
             line = list(color = "#00695c", width = 2, dash = "dash"))))
    }
    anns <- c(anns, list(
      list(x = if (alternative == "less") -tc else tc, y = ymax * 1.17,
           text = if (alternative == "two.sided") "crit. values (α = 0.05)" else "crit. value (α = 0.05)",
           showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "center",
           font = list(color = "#00695c", size = 11))))
  }
  if (!is.null(pval)) {
    side <- if (alternative == "less") -3.05 else 3.05
    anns <- c(anns, list(
      list(x = side, y = 0.085, text = paste0("p-value ≈ ", pval),
           showarrow = TRUE, ax = if (alternative == "less") -10 else 10, ay = -28,
           arrowcolor = "#b26a00", font = list(color = "#b26a00", size = 12))))
  }
  # shade each tail as its own trace so two-sided fills the tails (not the middle)
  add_shade <- function(pp, keep) add_trace(pp, x = x[keep], y = y[keep],
      type = "scatter", mode = "lines", fill = "tozeroy",
      fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.6)",
      line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)", width = 1),
      name = "shaded region", hoverinfo = "skip")
  p <- plot_ly(width = 520, height = 370) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 3.5),
              name = paste0("t(", df, ")"), hoverinfo = "skip")
  p <- if (alternative == "two.sided") add_shade(add_shade(p, x <= -cut), x >= cut) else add_shade(p, shade_keep)
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 14)),
      xaxis = list(title = "test statistic", range = xr,
                   zeroline = FALSE, fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero",
                   range = c(0, ymax * 1.3), fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 34, r = 12, t = 36, b = 42),
      showlegend = FALSE, shapes = shapes, annotations = anns
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}
```

<script>
document.addEventListener(
  "click",
  function (event) {
    /*
     * Before Quarto removes the Show Solution button,
     * save an exact copy of its HTML.
     */
    const solutionButton = event.target.closest(
      ".btn-exercise-solution"
    );

    if (solutionButton) {
      const buttonGroup = solutionButton.closest(
        ".btn-group-exercise-editor"
      );

      if (buttonGroup) {
        buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml =
          solutionButton.outerHTML;
      }

      return;
    }

    /*
     * Detect when the student presses Start Over.
     */
    const startOverButton = event.target.closest(
      '.btn-exercise-editor[aria-label="Start Over"]'
    );

    if (!startOverButton) return;

    const currentSlide = startOverButton.closest("section");

    const buttonGroup = startOverButton.closest(
      ".btn-group-exercise-editor"
    );

    if (!currentSlide || !buttonGroup) return;

    /*
     * Let Quarto perform its normal reset first.
     */
    window.setTimeout(function () {
      const solutions = currentSlide.querySelectorAll(
        ".exercise-solution"
      );

      /*
       * Hide the opened solution.
       */
      solutions.forEach(function (solution) {
        solution.classList.add("d-none");
      });

      /*
       * Restore Show Solution only when it is missing.
       */
      if (
        solutions.length === 0 ||
        buttonGroup.querySelector(".btn-exercise-solution") ||
        !buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml
      ) {
        return;
      }

      const holder = document.createElement("div");

      holder.innerHTML =
        buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml.trim();

      const restoredButton = holder.firstElementChild;

      if (!restoredButton) return;

      restoredButton.onclick = function () {
        solutions.forEach(function (solution) {
          solution.classList.remove("d-none");
        });

        restoredButton.remove();
      };

      buttonGroup.appendChild(restoredButton);
    }, 0);
  },
  true
);
</script>

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

Null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, and decisions.
:::

Tests for one mean, one proportion, and one variance.
:::

Tests comparing two independent means, proportions, or variances.
:::

Tests based on differences from matched or before-and-after observations.
:::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core skill</span>
Identify the parameter, then state $H_0$ and $H_a$ correctly.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core tool</span>
Use $Z$, $t$, $\chi^2$, and $F$ reference distributions for p-values.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core habit</span>
State the conclusion in context, without overclaiming a p-value.
:::
::::

---

## 6.1 What a Hypothesis Test Does

::: {.defbox .fragment}
<span class="label">High-Level Idea</span>
A hypothesis test uses sample evidence to determine whether there is enough evidence against a claim about a population parameter.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Null hypothesis, $H_0$</span>
The reference claim about the population parameter that is assumed true when calculating the test statistic and p-value.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Alternative hypothesis, $H_a$</span>
The competing claim supported when the sample provides sufficient evidence against $H_0$.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The test is performed **assuming $H_0$ is true**. The p-value measures how unusual the data are under that assumption.
:::

---

## The Six-Step Procedure

::: {.slide-stack}
<ol class="step-list">
  <li class="fragment"><strong>1. Check assumptions.</strong> Verify the sampling or experimental design, independence, and any Normal or large-sample conditions required by the test.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>2. Choose $\alpha$.</strong> Set the significance level before making the decision.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>3. State hypotheses.</strong> Use the correct population parameter.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>4. Compute the statistic.</strong> Standardize the estimate with the correct standard error.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>5. Find the p-value.</strong> Use the reference distribution and the tail area that matches $H_a$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>6. Conclude.</strong> Compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and write the conclusion in context.</li>
</ol>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The assumptions must be reasonable before using the stated reference distribution to calculate the test statistic and p-value.
:::
:::

---

## Choosing the Alternative

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Left-tailed</span>

$$
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad
H_a:\theta<\theta_0
$$

Use when the research question asks whether the parameter decreased or is smaller.

The null may equivalently be written as $H_0:\theta\ge\theta_0$.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Right-tailed</span>

$$
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad
H_a:\theta>\theta_0
$$

Use when the research question asks whether the parameter increased or is larger.

The null may equivalently be written as $H_0:\theta\le\theta_0$.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Two-sided</span>

$$
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad
H_a:\theta\ne\theta_0
$$

Use when the research question asks whether the parameter changed in either direction.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
For a one-sided test, calculations use the boundary value $\theta=\theta_0$. This is why the null is often written with equality even when the full null claim contains an inequality.
:::

---

## P-Value Areas {.pval-areas}

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
<ol class="step-list compact-steps">
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Left-tailed:</strong> $P(W \le w^*)$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Right-tailed:</strong> $P(W \ge w^*)$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Two-tailed $Z$ or $t$:</strong> double the tail area beyond $|w^*|$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Two-tailed $\chi^2$ or $F$:</strong> add the relevant lower- and upper-tail areas because the distributions are asymmetric.</li>
</ol>
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
Use the **two dropdowns** at the top-right of the plot: first pick the **type of test** ($Z$, $t$, $\chi^2$, or $F$), then pick the **alternative** (left-tailed, right-tailed, or two-tailed). Then **drag the dotted line** to move the observed test statistic — the shaded area and the p-value label below the plot update as you drag (for two-tailed $Z$ and $t$, the two boundaries move together).
:::
:::
::::

<p class="fragment" style="font-size:0.48em; color:var(--sta-muted); margin-top:3px; line-height:1.4; text-align:center;">$W$ is the test statistic from the chosen reference distribution (<em>Z</em>, <em>t</em>, chi-square, or <em>F</em>), with observed value $w^*$.</p>

::: {.dropdown-plot}
```{r}
test_dropdown()
```
:::

---

## Decision Rule

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.decision-cards}
::: {.defbox}
<span class="label">If p-value $\le \alpha$</span>
Reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_a$.
:::

::: {.defbox}
<span class="label">If p-value $> \alpha$</span>
Fail to reject $H_0$.
:::
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Careful language</span>
Failing to reject $H_0$ does **not** prove $H_0$. It only means the sample does not provide enough evidence against it at the chosen significance level.
:::
:::

---

## Reading Strength of Evidence

::: {.evidence-layout}
::: {.table-gap}
| p-value range | Textbook language |
|---|---|
| $\le 0.001$ | Very strong evidence against $H_0$ |
| $0.001$ to $0.01$ | Strong evidence |
| $0.01$ to $0.05$ | Evidence |
| $0.05$ to $0.075$ | Some evidence |
| $0.075$ to $0.10$ | Slight evidence |
| $>0.10$ | Little or no evidence against $H_0$ |
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .table-note}
Statistical significance does not measure practical importance. Pair the p-value with an estimate or confidence interval.
:::
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A test gives p-value $0.032$ and uses $\alpha=0.05$. What should we do?
:::

- Fail to reject $H_0$
- [Reject $H_0$]{.correct data-explanation="Because 0.032 is less than 0.05, the result is statistically significant at the 5% level."}
- Prove $H_0$ is false
- Increase $\alpha$ until the test works

---

## 6.2.1 Hypothesis Tests on the Mean, $\sigma$ Known

::: {.defbox}
For testing $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ when $\sigma$ is **known**, use the test statistic

$$
z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
$$

which, under $H_0$, follows the standard normal reference distribution $Z\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$z^*\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use when</span>
Testing a population mean with known $\sigma$ and an appropriate random/normal-or-large-sample setup.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Coffee Fill Volume

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
The cafe chain **Second Cup** advertises that a large iced latte is filled to a target of $\mu_0=7.2$ oz of base. Customers complain the cups feel light, so quality control pulls a random sample of $n=40$ cups.

From years of calibration records, the filling machine's standard deviation is known: $\sigma=1.1$ oz. The sample mean is $\bar{x}=6.7$ oz.

Test whether the true mean fill volume has **dropped below** 7.2 oz at $\alpha=0.05$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">What we are given</span>

- Target mean: $\mu_0 = 7.2$ oz
- Known SD: $\sigma = 1.1$ oz
- Sample: $n = 40$, $\bar{x} = 6.7$ oz
- Significance level: $\alpha = 0.05$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Which test?</span>
$\sigma$ is **known**, so this is a one-sample $z$ test with reference distribution $N(0,1)$.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Coffee Example: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\mu=7.2 \qquad H_a:\mu<7.2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=\frac{6.7-7.2}{1.1/\sqrt{40}}=-2.8748$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(Z\le -2.8748)=0.00202$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ztest_plot(zstar = -2.8748, zcrit = -1.645, alternative = "less",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "z* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.00202 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is sufficient evidence that the mean fill volume is below 7.2 oz.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Coffee z Test

```{webr}
n <- 40
xbar <- 6.7
mu0 <- 7.2
sigma <- 1.1

z_star <- (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
p_value <- pnorm(z_star)

z_star
p_value
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

In the coffee example, the alternative is $H_a:\mu<7.2$. Which p-value formula matches the test?
:::

- $P(Z\ge z^*)$
- [$P(Z\le z^*)$]{.correct data-explanation="A less-than alternative is left-tailed, so the p-value is the area to the left of the observed z statistic."}
- $2P(Z\ge z^*)$
- $P(Z=z^*)$

---

## 6.2.2 Hypothesis Tests on the Mean, $\sigma$ Unknown

::: {.defbox}
For testing $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ when $\sigma$ is **unknown**, replace it with $s$ and use the test statistic

$$
t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}
$$

which, under $H_0$, follows the Student $t$ distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$t^*\sim t_{n-1}$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>
Random/independent observations; population normal or sample large enough for the $t$ approximation.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Food Delivery ETA

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
The delivery app **Uber Eats** promises an average drop-off time of $16.5$ minutes. Suspecting their orders usually take longer, a student randomly selects 12 of their recent orders and records the wait time (in minutes):

`16.2, 18.4, 15.7, 19.1, 17.3, 16.9, 20.4, 18.2, 15.9, 17.6, 16.7, 19.8`

Test whether the true mean delivery time is **greater** than the advertised 16.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:\mu=16.5,\qquad H_a:\mu>16.5$$
$\sigma$ is unknown, so use a one-sample $t$ test.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">What we are given</span>

- Advertised mean: $\mu_0 = 16.5$ min
- Sample: $n = 12$
- Sample mean: $\bar{x} = 17.68$ min
- Sample SD: $s = 1.53$ min
- Significance level: $\alpha = 0.05$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Which test?</span>
$\sigma$ is **unknown** and estimated by $s$, so use a one-sample $t$ test with reference distribution [$t_{11}$.]{style="white-space:nowrap"}
:::
:::
::::

---

## Food Delivery ETA: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\mu=16.5 \qquad H_a:\mu>16.5 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}=\frac{17.68-16.5}{1.53/\sqrt{12}}=2.682$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(T_{11}\ge 2.682)=0.0107$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ttest_plot(tstar = 2.682, tcrit = 1.796, df = 11, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "t* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0107 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is evidence that the student's mean delivery time exceeds the advertised $16.5$ minutes.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Food Delivery ETA

```{webr}
waits <- c(16.2, 18.4, 15.7, 19.1, 17.3, 16.9,
           20.4, 18.2, 15.9, 17.6, 16.7, 19.8)

t.test(waits, alternative = "greater", mu = 16.5)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The output gives $t=2.682$, $df=11$, and p-value $0.0107$. At $\alpha=0.05$, reject $H_0$.
:::

---

## 6.2.3 Hypothesis Tests on a Proportion {.compact}

::: {.defbox style="padding: 0.65rem 0.9rem; margin-bottom: 0.55rem;"}
For testing $H_0:p=p_0$, use

$$
z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}},
$$

which follows the standard Normal reference distribution under $H_0$.
:::

:::: {.two-col style="gap: 0.75rem;"}
::: {.notebox .fragment style="padding: 0.7rem 0.9rem;"}
<span class="label">Reference Distribution</span>

$$
z^*\sim N(0,1)
$$

<span class="label">Use the Null Value</span>

The standard error uses $p_0$, not $\hat p$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment style="padding: 0.7rem 0.9rem;"}
<span class="label">Required Conditions</span>

- Use a random sample or randomized design.
- Observations should be independent.
- When sampling without replacement, ensure $n\leq 0.10N$.

<span class="label">Large-Count Condition</span>

Under $H_0$, check

$$
np_0\geq 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n(1-p_0)\geq 10.
$$
:::
::::

---

## Example: Reusable Cup Discount

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
Last year only $10\%$ of students used the reusable-cup discount at a campus cafe. After a sustainability campaign, a fresh random survey finds $x=68$ of $n=520$ students bringing their own cup.

Is this evidence that the participation rate has **increased** above $10\%$?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:p=0.10,\qquad H_a:p>0.10$$

$$\hat p=\frac{68}{520}=0.1308$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">What we are given</span>

- Null proportion: $p_0 = 0.10$
- Sample: $n = 520$, $x = 68$
- Sample proportion: $\hat p = 0.1308$
- Significance level: $\alpha = 0.05$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Which test?</span>
Since $np_0 = 52$ and $n(1-p_0) = 468$ are both $\ge 10$, use a one-sample $z$ test for a proportion with reference distribution $N(0,1)$.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Reusable Cup Discount: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:p=0.10 \qquad H_a:p>0.10 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}=\frac{0.1308-0.10}{\sqrt{0.10\cdot 0.90/520}}=2.339$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.339)=0.0097$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ztest_plot(zstar = 2.339, zcrit = 1.645, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "z* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0097 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is evidence the participation rate has increased above $10\%$.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Reusable Cup Discount

```{webr}
x <- 68
n <- 520
p0 <- 0.10

# z test: build the statistic by hand and use the N(0,1) tail
phat <- x / n
z_star <- (phat - p0) / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
p_value <- 1 - pnorm(z_star)

phat
z_star
p_value

# Alternative Way: infer::prop_test() reports the z statistic directly
# with z = TRUE (it should match z_star above). The yes/no outcomes are
# fully determined by x and n, so we rebuild them from the counts:
library(infer)
cups <- data.frame(
  reusable = factor(c(rep("yes", x), rep("no", n - x)),
                    levels = c("yes", "no"))
)

prop_test(cups, reusable ~ NULL, success = "yes",
          p = p0, alternative = "greater", z = TRUE)
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

For the reusable-cup test, why is the alternative $H_a:p>0.10$?
:::

- The sample proportion is always greater than the null value
- [The research question asks whether participation has increased]{.correct data-explanation="An increase means the population proportion is larger than the old value 0.10, so the test is right-tailed."}
- The sample size is greater than 30
- Proportion tests are always right-tailed

---

## 6.2.4 Hypothesis Tests on a Variance

::: {.defbox}
For one normal population, test a variance using the chi-square statistic:

$$
\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$\chi^2$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Important condition</span>
The population should be approximately normal. Variance tests are sensitive to non-normality.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Protein Scoop Consistency

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
A fitness brand claims its protein powder is dosed so precisely that scoop weights have standard deviation at most $2.8$ g. A reviewer weighs a random sample of $n=28$ scoops and finds $s=3.4$ g.

Does this **undermine** the consistency claim? Use $\alpha=0.05$ and assume scoop weights are normal.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:\sigma^2\le 2.8^2,\qquad H_a:\sigma^2>2.8^2$$

For the test statistic, evaluate the null hypothesis at its boundary, $\sigma_0^2=2.8^2$. A larger sample spread is evidence against the "at most 2.8 g" claim.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">What we are given</span>

- Claimed SD: $\sigma_0 = 2.8$ g, so $\sigma_0^2 = 7.84$
- Sample: $n = 28$, $s = 3.4$ g
- Degrees of freedom: $df = n-1 = 27$
- Significance level: $\alpha = 0.05$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Which test?</span>
Testing a claim about a single variance (normal population), so use a one-sample $\chi^2$ test with reference distribution $\chi^2_{27}$.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Protein Scoop Consistency: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\sigma^2\le 2.8^2 \qquad H_a:\sigma^2>2.8^2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}=\frac{27\cdot 3.4^2}{2.8^2}=39.81$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(\chi^2_{27}\ge 39.81)=0.0534$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
chisq_test_plot(chistar = 39.81, chicrit = 40.11, df = 27, alternative = "greater",
                shade = "reject",
                title = "χ²* falls short of the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0534 > 0.05$ (and $39.81 < 40.11$), so **fail to reject** $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is not enough evidence that the true SD of scoop weights exceeds $2.8$ g.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Scoop Variance Test

```{webr}
n <- 28
s <- 3.4
sigma0 <- 2.8

chi_star <- (n - 1) * s^2 / sigma0^2
p_value <- 1 - pchisq(chi_star, df = n - 1)

chi_star
p_value
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Base R has no one-sample variance test, so the code builds $\chi^{2*}$ by hand from $n$ and $s$ and finds the p-value with `pchisq()`.
:::

---

## 6.3 Two-Sample Test Targets

| Target parameter | Typical question | Reference distribution |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu_1-\mu_2$ | Are two population means different? | $Z$ or $t$ |
| $p_1-p_2$ | Are two population proportions different? | $Z$ or $\chi^2$|
| $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ | Are two population variances different? | $F$ |

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .spaced-note}
These tests all compare **two independent samples**.
:::

---

## 6.3.1 Two Means, $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ Known

::: {.defbox}
When both population standard deviations, $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$, are **known**, use the test statistic

$$
z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}}
$$

which, under $H_0$, follows the standard normal reference distribution $Z\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$z^*\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use when</span>
Comparing two population means from independent samples with **known** $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$. Usually $D_0=0$.
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Two Independent Means

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Sampling structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two samples are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If sampling without replacement, each sample is less than 10% of its population.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Model condition</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Each population is approximately normal, or both sample sizes are large enough for the CLT.</li>
  <li class="fragment">For a pooled test, equal population variances should be reasonable.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## Example: Comparing Download Speeds

::: {.examplebox}
Two campus internet providers both advertise fast service. From years of monitoring, download speeds (Mbps) are known to have $\sigma_A=12$ for Provider A and $\sigma_B=15$ for Provider B.

A student runs independent speed tests at randomly selected times under comparable campus conditions and records:

- Provider A: $n_A=40$, $\bar{x}_A=86$ Mbps
- Provider B: $n_B=45$, $\bar{x}_B=79$ Mbps

Is Provider A's mean download speed **higher** than Provider B's?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Let $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ be the population mean download speeds under these campus testing conditions. Test $H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0$ against $H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B>0$.

Both population SDs are **known**, so use a two-sample $z$ test.
:::

---

## Download Speeds: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B)-0}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2/n_A+\sigma_B^2/n_B}}=\frac{86-79}{\sqrt{12^2/40+15^2/45}}=2.387$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.387)=0.0085$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ztest_plot(zstar = 2.387, zcrit = 1.645, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "z* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0085 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is evidence Provider A's mean download speed is higher than Provider B's.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Download Speeds

```{webr}
# Population SDs known -> build the two-sample z by hand
nA <- 40; xbarA <- 86; sigmaA <- 12
nB <- 45; xbarB <- 79; sigmaB <- 15
se <- sqrt(sigmaA^2 / nA + sigmaB^2 / nB)
z_star <- (xbarA - xbarB) / se
p_value <- 1 - pnorm(z_star)   # Ha: muA - muB > 0
z_star
p_value

# Alternative Way: Same test straight from summary statistics with the BSDA package:
library(BSDA)
zsum.test(mean.x = xbarA, sigma.x = sigmaA, n.x = nA,
          mean.y = xbarB, sigma.y = sigmaB, n.y = nB,
          mu = 0, alternative = "greater")
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The output gives $z^*=2.39$ and p-value $0.0085$. At $\alpha=0.05$, reject $H_0$.
:::

---

## 6.3.2 Two Means, Equal Unknown Variances

::: {.defbox}
When the population variances are unknown but can be assumed **equal**, pool the two sample variances into one estimate:

$$
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2},
\qquad
t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{s_p\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1}+\dfrac{1}{n_2}}}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Degrees of freedom</span>
$df=n_1+n_2-2$ under the equal-variance model. Welch's test instead uses an estimated degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">When to pool</span>
Reasonable when the sample spreads are similar — e.g. the fold rule $\dfrac{\max(s_1,s_2)}{\min(s_1,s_2)}<\sqrt{2}$.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Two Fertilizers, Similar Spread

::: {.examplebox}
A gardener randomly assigns independent tomato plots to one of two organic fertilizers and expects the two groups to have **similar variability**. The resulting yields (kg per plant) are:

Fertilizer A: `4.2 3.8 4.5 4.0 3.9 4.3 4.1 3.7 4.4`

Fertilizer B: `3.6 3.9 3.4 3.8 3.5 3.7 3.3 4.0 3.6 3.5`

Do the two fertilizers give **different** mean yields at $\alpha=0.05$?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Let $\mu_A,\mu_B$ be the true mean yields. Test $H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0$ against $H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq 0$.

Variances are unknown but the spreads look similar, so use a pooled two-sample $t$ test.
:::

---

## Two Fertilizers: Calculation {.tight-calc}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq 0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Pooled variance</span>
$$s_p^2=\frac{(n_A-1)s_A^2+(n_B-1)s_B^2}{n_A+n_B-2}=\frac{8(0.274^2)+9(0.221^2)}{17}=0.0612$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$t^*=\frac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_A+1/n_B}}=\frac{4.10-3.63}{0.2475\sqrt{1/9+1/10}}=4.13$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=2\,P(T_{17}\ge 4.13)=0.0007$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ttest_plot(tstar = 4.13, tcrit = 2.11, df = 17, alternative = "two.sided",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "t* falls in the rejection region (two-sided, α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0007 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is strong evidence the two fertilizers give different mean yields.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Two Fertilizers

```{webr}
fert_a <- c(4.2, 3.8, 4.5, 4.0, 3.9, 4.3, 4.1, 3.7, 4.4)
fert_b <- c(3.6, 3.9, 3.4, 3.8, 3.5, 3.7, 3.3, 4.0, 3.6, 3.5)

# Equal variances assumed -> pooled two-sample t test
t.test(fert_a, fert_b, var.equal = TRUE)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The output gives $t^*=4.13$, $df=17$, and p-value $0.0007$. At $\alpha=0.05$, reject $H_0$.
:::

---

## 6.3.3 Two Means, Unequal or Unspecified Variances

::: {.defbox}
For unequal or unspecified population variances, use Welch's two-sample $t$ test (no pooling), with test statistic

$$
t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}
$$

which, under $H_0$, approximately follows a $t$ reference distribution with the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$T\sim t_\nu$, with the Welch–Satterthwaite $\nu$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use when</span>
Comparing two population means from independent samples when equal variances are not clearly justified.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Active Recall vs Rereading

::: {.examplebox}
Twenty-two students are randomly assigned to prepare for the same quiz using either **active recall** (self-testing) or passive rereading.

Active recall: `88 84 90 86 89 85 88 83 90 86 89 85`

Rereading: `84 86 83 85 84 82 87 84 86 85`

Does active recall produce a higher mean quiz score?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Let $\mu_1$ be the active-recall mean and $\mu_2$ the rereading mean. Test $H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0$ against $H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0$.
:::

---

## Active Recall vs Rereading: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic (no pooling)</span>
$$t^*=\frac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}=\frac{86.92-84.60}{\sqrt{2.392^2/12+1.506^2/10}}=2.76$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(T_\nu\ge 2.76)=0.0062,\qquad \nu\approx 18.8$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ttest_plot(tstar = 2.76, tcrit = 1.73, df = 19, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "t* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0062 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is evidence active recall produces a higher mean quiz score than rereading.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Active Recall vs Rereading

```{webr}
active <- c(88, 84, 90, 86, 89, 85, 88, 83, 90, 86, 89, 85)
review <- c(84, 86, 83, 85, 84, 82, 87, 84, 86, 85)

t.test(active, review, alternative = "greater", var.equal = FALSE)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Welch's test reports $t^*=2.76$ with $\nu\approx 18.8$ and p-value $0.0062$. At $\alpha=0.05$, reject $H_0$.
:::

---

## 6.3.4 Hypothesis Tests on Two Proportions

::: {.defbox}
When testing $H_0:p_1-p_2=0$, pool the sample proportions under the null and use the test statistic

$$
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2},
\qquad
z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}
$$

which, under $H_0$, follows the standard normal reference distribution $Z\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$z^*\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use when</span>
Comparing two population proportions from independent samples, with enough successes and failures in each group.
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Difference of Proportions

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Sampling structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two groups are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If sampling without replacement, each sample should be less than 10% of its population.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Large-count condition under $H_0$</span>

For testing $H_0:p_1=p_2$, first calculate the pooled proportion:

$$
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}.
$$

Then check the expected successes and failures in both groups:

$$
n_i\hat p\ge 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_i(1-\hat p)\ge 10,
\qquad i=1,2.
$$
:::
::::

---

## Example: Push Notifications

::: {.examplebox}
A habit-tracking app runs an experiment by randomly assigning half of its new users to receive a daily push notification and the other half to receive none. For each user, the app records whether they completed a workout that day.

Push notification: $142$ check-ins out of $360$ users

No notification: $118$ check-ins out of $370$ users

Test whether the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$
H_0:p_1-p_2=0,\qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0
$$
:::

---

## Push Notifications: Calculation {.tight-calc}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:p_1-p_2=0 \qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Sample and pooled proportions</span>
$$\hat p_1=\tfrac{142}{360}=0.394,\quad \hat p_2=\tfrac{118}{370}=0.319,\quad \hat p=\tfrac{142+118}{360+370}=0.356$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}=\frac{0.0756}{0.0354}=2.13$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.13)=0.0166$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ztest_plot(zstar = 2.13, zcrit = 1.645, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "z* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.0166 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is evidence the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Two Proportions

```{webr}
library(infer)

# Rebuild each group's yes/no check-in outcomes from the counts
notifications <- data.frame(
  group = factor(rep(c("push", "none"), c(360, 370)),
                 levels = c("push", "none")),
  checkin = factor(c(rep("yes", 142), rep("no", 360 - 142),
                     rep("yes", 118), rep("no", 370 - 118)),
                   levels = c("yes", "no"))
)

# infer::prop_test() reports the z statistic directly with z = TRUE
prop_test(notifications, checkin ~ group, success = "yes",
          order = c("push", "none"), alternative = "greater", z = TRUE)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
`infer::prop_test()` with `z = TRUE` reports the **z statistic directly** ($z^*\approx 2.13$) with p-value $0.0166$, so there is evidence the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.
:::

---

## 6.3.5 Hypothesis Tests on Two Variances

::: {.defbox}
For two normal populations, test a ratio of variances with the test statistic

$$
F^*=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
$$

which, under $H_0$, follows an $F$ reference distribution with $n_1-1$ and $n_2-1$ degrees of freedom.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$F^*\sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use when</span>
Comparing two population variances from independent **normal** samples; the $F$ test is sensitive to non-normality.
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Ratio of Variances

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Required structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two samples are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample comes from a random process or randomized design.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Normality matters here</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The $F$ test for a variance ratio is sensitive to non-normality.</li>
  <li class="fragment">This condition is more important here than it is for many mean-based tests.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## Example: Scoring Consistency

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
Two basketball players average about the same points per game, but a scout suspects **Player A is less consistent** — more variable game to game.

Player A: `76 87 74 86 81 83 77 88 79 84 75 82`

Player B: `82 84 79 85 81 83 80 86 82 84`

Test whether Player A has the larger scoring variance at $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:\sigma_A^2=\sigma_B^2,\qquad H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2$$

$$F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}\sim F_{n_A-1,\,n_B-1}$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.card}
<span class="label">What we are given</span>

- Player A: $n_A = 12$, $s_A^2 = 23.09$
- Player B: $n_B = 10$, $s_B^2 = 4.933$
- Degrees of freedom: $df = (11,\ 9)$
- Significance level: $\alpha = 0.05$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Which test?</span>
Comparing two population variances from normal populations, so use an $F$ test. Because the alternative is $H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2$, Player A is placed in the numerator:

$$F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}\sim F_{11,\,9}.$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Scoring Consistency: Calculation

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>
$$H_0:\sigma_A^2=\sigma_B^2 \qquad H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>
$$F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}=\frac{23.09}{4.933}=4.68$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>
$$\text{p-value}=P(F_{11,9}\ge 4.68)=0.014$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ftest_plot(fstar = 4.68, fcrit = 3.10, df1 = 11, df2 = 9, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "F* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.014 \le 0.05$ (and $4.68 > 3.10$), so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is strong evidence Player A has the larger scoring variance (i.e. is less consistent).
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Ratio of Variances

```{webr}
player_a <- c(76, 87, 74, 86, 81, 83, 77, 88, 79, 84, 75, 82)
player_b <- c(82, 84, 79, 85, 81, 83, 80, 86, 82, 84)

var.test(player_a, player_b, alternative = "greater")
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
`var.test` reports $F^*$, the two degrees of freedom, and the p-value. An $F^*$ well above 1 is evidence that Player A's scoring is more variable.
:::

---

## 6.4 Paired Data

::: {.defbox}
For matched pairs or before-after data, reduce each pair to a difference (measurement 1 $-$ measurement 2):

$$
d_i = m_{1i}-m_{2i} \quad (\text{or } m_{2i}-m_{1i})
$$

Then run a one-sample $t$ test on $\mu_d$.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Not independent groups</span>
The two measurements inside a pair are linked.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$t$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom for the differences.
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Paired Data

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Paired structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Each pair comes from the same unit, matched units, or a before-after measurement.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Analyze the differences $d_i$, not the two original columns separately.</li>
  <li class="fragment">The pairs themselves must be independent of one another.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Sampling and model conditions</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The pairs should come from a random sample or randomized experiment.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If sampling without replacement, the number of pairs should not exceed $10\%$ of the population.</li>
  <li class="fragment">For a small sample, the distribution of the differences should be approximately normal.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## Example: Pomodoro Focus Timer

::: {.examplebox}
Each of 12 students completes a timed practice set, then writes a comparable set after a week of studying with the **Pomodoro** technique (25-minute focus blocks). Scores are paired within each student.

Before: `34 29 41 38 36 33 40 31 37 35 39 32`

After: `37 28 45 39 38 33 38 34 38 39 41 33`

Is there evidence that the students' mean score is higher after the week of Pomodoro study than before?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Use paired differences $d_i=\text{after}_i-\text{before}_i$ and test $H_0:\mu_d=0$ against $H_a:\mu_d>0$.
:::

---

## Pomodoro: Difference Table {.compact-table .pomodoro-paired}

<style>
.reveal section.pomodoro-paired .intro-note {
  font-size: 0.60em;
  line-height: 1.14;
  padding: 9px 13px;
  margin-bottom: 7px;
}

.reveal section.pomodoro-paired table {
  font-size: 0.57em;
  line-height: 1.04;
}

.reveal section.pomodoro-paired th,
.reveal section.pomodoro-paired td {
  padding: 3px 7px;
}

.reveal section.pomodoro-paired .paired-calc {
  font-size: 0.60em;
  line-height: 1.11;
  padding: 11px 14px;
  margin-bottom: 8px;
}

.reveal section.pomodoro-paired .paired-result {
  font-size: 0.60em;
  line-height: 1.16;
  padding: 10px 14px;
  margin-bottom: 0;
}

.reveal section.pomodoro-paired mjx-container[display="true"] {
  margin: 0.18em 0 !important;
}
</style>

::: {.intro-note}
Reduce each pair ($M_1$ = before, $M_2$ = after) to $d_i = M_2 - M_1$, then analyze the 12 differences as one sample.
:::

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
| Person | $M_1$ | $M_2$ | $d_i = M_2-M_1$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | 34 | 37 | 3 |
| 2 | 29 | 28 | −1 |
| 3 | 41 | 45 | 4 |
| 4 | 38 | 39 | 1 |
| 5 | 36 | 38 | 2 |
| 6 | 33 | 33 | 0 |
| 7 | 40 | 38 | −2 |
| 8 | 31 | 34 | 3 |
| 9 | 37 | 38 | 1 |
| 10 | 35 | 39 | 4 |
| 11 | 39 | 41 | 2 |
| 12 | 32 | 33 | 1 |
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .paired-calc}
<span class="label">Mean and SD of the differences</span>

$$
\bar d=\frac{18}{12}=1.5,
\qquad
s_d=\sqrt{\frac{39}{11}}=1.88
$$

<span class="label">Test statistic</span>

$$
t^*
=
\frac{\bar d-0}{s_d/\sqrt n}
=
\frac{1.5}{1.88/\sqrt{12}}
=
2.76,
\qquad df=11
$$

<span class="label">p-value</span>

$$
P(T_{11}\ge 2.76)\approx 0.0093
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .paired-result}
<span class="label">Decision and conclusion</span>

Since $0.0093\le 0.05$, reject $H_0$.

There is evidence that the students' mean score is higher after the week of Pomodoro study than before.
:::
:::
::::

## Check in R: Paired Pomodoro Test

```{webr}
before <- c(34, 29, 41, 38, 36, 33, 40, 31, 37, 35, 39, 32)
after <- c(37, 28, 45, 39, 38, 33, 38, 34, 38, 39, 41, 33)

t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
```

::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
ttest_plot(tstar = 2.76, tcrit = 1.796, df = 11, alternative = "greater",
           shade = "reject",
           title = "t* falls in the rejection region (α = 0.05)")
```
:::

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

In the Pomodoro example, why is a paired $t$ test appropriate?
:::

- The two samples have the same mean
- The sample size is less than 30
- [Each student has both before and after scores, so observations are matched within student]{.correct data-explanation="The student creates a natural pair: the before score and after score come from the same person."}
- Proportion tests cannot use score data

---

## Choosing the Right Test

| If the problem asks for... | Use... |
|---|---|
| one mean and gives $\sigma$ | one-sample $z$ test |
| one mean and gives $s$ or raw data | one-sample $t$ test |
| one proportion | one-proportion $z$ test |
| one variance | chi-square test |
| difference of means, known $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ | two-sample $z$ test |
| difference of means, equal variances | pooled two-sample $t$ test |
| difference of means, unequal/unspecified variances | Welch two-sample $t$ test |
| difference of proportions | two-proportion $z$ test |
| ratio of variances | $F$ test |
| before-after or matched data | paired $t$ test on differences |

---

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A problem gives raw before-and-after blood pressure measurements on the same 12 patients. Which test should you use?
:::

- Two independent sample $t$ test
- One-proportion $z$ test
- [Paired $t$ test on the differences]{.correct data-explanation="Before-and-after measurements on the same patient are paired. First compute each patient's difference, then use a one-sample t test on those differences."}
- $F$ test for variances

---

## Test Statistic Cheat Sheet {.cheat-sheet}

| Situation | Test statistic |
|---|---|
| One mean, $\sigma$ known | $z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$ |
| One mean, $\sigma$ unknown | $t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$ |
| One proportion | $z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$ |
| One variance | $\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}$ |
| Two means, $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ known | $z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}}$ |
| Two means, pooled $t$ | $t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}}$ |
| Pooled variance ($s_p^2$) | $s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}$ |
| Two means, Welch $t$ | $t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}$ |
| Two proportions | $z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}$ |
| Ratio of variances | $F^*=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}$ |
| Paired differences | $t^*=\frac{\bar{d}-\mu_{d0}}{s_d/\sqrt n}$ |

---

## What to Write in a Conclusion

:::: {.conclusion-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
Reject or fail to reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Evidence strength</span>
Use the p-value to describe how strong the evidence is.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Context</span>
Name the population parameter and the direction of the claim.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .spaced-note}
Good conclusion: "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill volume for large coffees is below 7.2 oz."
:::


---

## Chapter Summary {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Test Logic</span>
State $H_0$ and $H_a$, calculate a test statistic, find the p-value, and compare it with $\alpha$ to make a decision.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Test Selection</span>
Choose the procedure from the parameter, the number and relationship of the samples, and whether the required assumptions are reasonable.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Interpretation</span>
Reject or fail to reject $H_0$, then state the evidence in context without claiming that $H_0$ was proved or disproved.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** Identify the parameter and study design first, choose the correct reference distribution, and let the p-value guide a careful contextual conclusion.
:::
